title: Keely Hodgkinson breaks 800m indoor world record with time of 1:54:87s
content:
Keely Hodgkinson ran 1:54:87s in Lievin, France, to break the long-standing women’s 800m indoor world record on Thursday.

Her performance was almost an entire second faster than Jolanda Ceplak’s time of 1:55.82s from the 2002 European indoor Championships, with that run incidentally being on the day Hodgkinson was born.

She remained consistent following a fast start (26.47s for the opening 200m lap), splitting 29.09s, 29.50s and 29.82s for the final three laps. Hodgkinson hit 400m in 55.56s, at which point the pacemaker dropped out, and a gap started to grow between the Briton and Swiss athlete Audrey Werro, the 2025 Diamond League winner over 800m.

Hodgkinson held her form to break an indoor world record which had stood for nearly 24 years, running a time she has only bettered twice outdoors.

“Thank god,” Hodgkinson said of her immediate feelings in a post-race interview on the track. “That was really fun, I’ve been looking forward to this.”

Also in the field was the 2024 World Indoor Champion and Olympic silver medallist Tsige Duguma, who finished third in 1:58.83s, half a second back on second-place Werro (1:58.38s).

Hodgkinson arrived in northern France just after running 1:56.33s at the British Indoor Championships. With that gun-to-tape performance, she bettered her own national record (previously 1:57.18s), took an early world lead for 2026, moved up to third all-time on the indoor list, and got within half a second off Ceplak. This was even better.

“Last couple of years, I wanted to run these fast times and now I am definitely in the shape to do so,” she said in her pre-race press conference. “It’s not just about the World Record but how fast we can really go.

“I surprise myself every time, I don’t really know what my limits are,” she continued. “But I am excited to see how far we can push it. These times 1:54s and 1:55s are becoming a regular occurrence (in women’s 800m). More and more people are running them, so we definitely can do some great things in the future. I hopefully have ten more years in me.”

The 23-year-old Briton adds the world record to an illustrious career achievements list. She won the Olympic title two summers ago in Paris, going unbeaten throughout 2024, a year which also included a European title, and a 1:54.61s British record when she won at the London Diamond League. That latter performance remains her best, as she sits sixth on the all-time list outdoors.

The 2025 season was an injury-hit one for Hodgkinson. She had plans to attack Ceplak’s indoor world record in February — saying she felt “in the best shape of my life” — but was forced to abandon those because of a hamstring problem.

Subsequently she had scratched racing the 800m at her home Diamond League meet in London in July, and only opened her season in mid-August — dropping a world-leading 1:54.74s time in Chorzow, Poland, her second-quickest ever.

It meant that, last September, Hodgkinson arrived at the World Championships in Tokyo, Japan, after only racing twice on the circuit. She ran 1:54.91s there, a time which ranks in the top 20 women’s 800m performances ever, though she took home bronze after being beaten by fellow Briton (and training partner) Georgia Hunter-Bell, who finished one hundredth quicker, as Kenya’s Lilian Odira won by three-tenths of a second in a championship-record time (1:54.62s).

This performance in Lievin — her second record-breaking indoor run, after producing the fastest ‘short track’ 600m in 2023 with a 1:23.41s time — sets Hodgkinson up for the World Indoor Championships in Torun, Poland, which take place in a month’s time.

That will be a competition debut for the Manchester-born middle-distance athlete. Injuries have kept her out of the past three editions. “I am looking forward to, hopefully, making it there, competing, and getting my first world title,” she said before her record attempt.

Then, in the summer, Hodgkinson will try to close the 1.33s gap between her and Jarmila Kratochvilova’s 1:53.28s outdoor world record from 1983.

There is also a home European Championships in Birmingham in August for her to defend her continental crown at, plus the Commonwealth Games are being hosted in Glasgow, Scotland, at the end of July which sets up the possibility of a championship double.
